title: Trigonometric Ratios
subject: mathematics

theory.introduction: Trigonometry begins with a simple question: if we know something about an angle in a right triangle, what can that angle tell us about the triangle's side lengths? Trigonometric ratios give us the answer. They connect angles to side lengths through three fundamental relationships: sine, cosine, and tangent. In this lesson, we build those ideas from the beginning, explain why the ratios work, learn how to choose the correct ratio, and use them to find unknown side lengths.

content.text: The word trigonometry comes from Greek roots meaning triangle measurement. At its most basic level, trigonometry studies relationships between angles and lengths in triangles.

Suppose you are looking at a ladder leaning against a wall. You may know the ladder's length and the angle it makes with the ground, but you want to know how high it reaches. Trigonometry gives you a systematic way to connect the angle with the unknown length.
The first important setting for trigonometry is the right triangle. Once we understand right triangles, we can define three ratios: sine, cosine, and tangent.
A right triangle is a triangle containing one angle of \(90^\circ\). The side opposite the right angle is called the hypotenuse.
The other two sides are called the legs. These sides, together with the angles, create predictable relationships. Trigonometric ratios describe those relationships.
For this lesson, we focus on the two acute angles of a right triangle. An acute angle is an angle greater than \(0^\circ\) and less than \(90^\circ\).

sections.title: The Three Sides of a Right Triangle

content.text: Before using any trigonometric ratio, you must be able to identify three sides: the hypotenuse, the opposite side, and the adjacent side.
The hypotenuse is always opposite the \(90^\circ\) angle. It is also the longest side of a right triangle.
The opposite side is the side directly across from the particular acute angle you are studying.
The adjacent side is the leg that touches the chosen angle. It is important that we do not call the hypotenuse the adjacent side in this context.
Opposite and adjacent are relative names. If you change the angle you are studying, the opposite and adjacent sides can switch roles.
The reason trigonometric ratios are so powerful comes from similar triangles. Two triangles are similar when they have the same shape, even if one is larger or smaller.
If two right triangles have the same acute angle, their corresponding angles are equal, so their corresponding side lengths are proportional.

For example, imagine one triangle is exactly twice as large as another. Every side is multiplied by \(2\). A ratio such as \( rac{	ext{opposite}}{	ext{hypotenuse}}\) does not change because both the numerator and denominator are multiplied by the same number.
This means a particular acute angle is associated with a particular set of side ratios. That is the central idea behind trigonometry.

sections.title: From an Angle to a Ratio

content.text: A triangle's actual side lengths tell us its size. Ratios tell us about its shape. This distinction is extremely useful.

Consider two right triangles with the same acute angle. One could have sides \(3,4,5\), while another could have sides \(6,8,10\). The second is twice as large, but the side proportions are identical.
For the corresponding sides, \( rac{3}{5}= rac{6}{10}= rac{4}{5}\). The numerical value of a ratio therefore depends on the angle and the shape, not on the overall size of the triangle.
The first fundamental trigonometric ratio is sine, written as \(\sin(	heta)\). Here \(	heta\) represents the acute angle we have chosen.
Sine compares the length of the opposite side with the length of the hypotenuse:
\[\sin(	heta)= rac{	ext{opposite}}{	ext{hypotenuse}}\]
Because the hypotenuse is the longest side, the opposite side is shorter than it for an acute angle. Therefore, for an acute angle, sine has a value between \(0\) and \(1\).
If the angle becomes larger, the opposite side becomes larger relative to the hypotenuse, so the sine ratio increases.
The second fundamental ratio is cosine, written as \(\cos(	heta)\). Cosine compares the adjacent side with the hypotenuse.
Its definition is:
\[\cos(	heta)= rac{	ext{adjacent}}{	ext{hypotenuse}}\]
For an acute angle, the adjacent side is shorter than the hypotenuse, so cosine is also between \(0\) and \(1\).
As the chosen angle increases, the adjacent side becomes smaller relative to the hypotenuse. Consequently, cosine decreases for acute angles.
The third fundamental ratio is tangent, written as \(	an(	heta)\). Unlike sine and cosine, tangent does not involve the hypotenuse.
Its definition is:
\[	an(	heta)= rac{	ext{opposite}}{	ext{adjacent}}\]
Tangent compares the two legs of the right triangle. Because either leg can be longer than the other, tangent can be less than \(1\), equal to \(1\), or greater than \(1\).
Tangent is closely connected with the steepness of a right triangle: a larger acute angle corresponds to a larger opposite-to-adjacent ratio.
SOH-CAH-TOA is a memory aid for the three definitions.
SOH means Sine = Opposite over Hypotenuse: \(\sin(	heta)= rac{O}{H}\).
CAH means Cosine = Adjacent over Hypotenuse: \(\cos(	heta)= rac{A}{H}\).
TOA means Tangent = Opposite over Adjacent: \(	an(	heta)= rac{O}{A}\).
The mnemonic is useful, but understanding what each ratio compares is more important than memorising three letters.
A ratio is a comparison. Saying \(\sin(	heta)=0.6\) means the opposite side is \(0.6\) times the length of the hypotenuse.
Similarly, \(\cos(	heta)=0.8\) means the adjacent side is \(0.8\) times the hypotenuse. And \(	an(	heta)=0.75\) means the opposite side is \(0.75\) times the adjacent side.
This way of thinking is more useful than treating sine, cosine, and tangent as mysterious calculator buttons. Each one is simply a particular comparison of two sides.

sections.title: How to Choose the Correct Ratio

content.text: The hardest part for many beginners is not the calculation; it is choosing the correct ratio. Use the information in the problem to decide.
If the two relevant sides are opposite and hypotenuse, use sine. If they are adjacent and hypotenuse, use cosine. If they are opposite and adjacent, use tangent.

A dependable four-step method is: first mark the angle you are using; second label the sides O, A, and H; third identify the known and unknown sides; fourth choose the ratio containing exactly those two sides.
Do not choose a ratio simply because you remember it. Choose it because its numerator and denominator match the sides involved in the problem.
When the required side lengths are known, calculating a trigonometric ratio is just substitution.

The same process works for cosine and tangent: identify the sides, write the correct ratio, substitute, and simplify.

sections.title: Using a Ratio to Find an Unknown Side

content.text: Trigonometry becomes especially useful when one side is unknown. If you know an acute angle and one suitable side, a trigonometric ratio can connect the known and unknown lengths.
For example, suppose \(	heta=60^\circ\), the adjacent side is \(5\,	ext{cm}\), and the hypotenuse is \(h\). Because the known and unknown sides are adjacent and hypotenuse, use cosine:
Since \(\cos(60^\circ)= rac{1}{2}\), we have \( rac{1}{2}= rac{5}{h}\). Multiplying both sides by \(h\) gives \( rac{h}{2}=5\), so \(h=10\,	ext{cm}\).
The important idea is not the particular angle. It is the structure: choose the ratio, substitute the known values, then rearrange the equation to isolate the unknown.
Once a ratio is written as an equation, solving for a side is ordinary algebra.
For example, if \(\sin(	heta)= rac{x}{12}\), multiply both sides by \(12\): \(x=12\sin(	heta)\).
If \(\cos(	heta)= rac{7}{x}\), multiply both sides by \(x\) and then divide by \(\cos(	heta)\): \(x= rac{7}{\cos(	heta)}\).
Do not try to memorise every possible rearrangement. Write the original ratio first and use algebra to solve it.

sections.title: A Complete Strategy for Right-Triangle Problems

content.text: A good solution begins before you touch the calculator. Draw or inspect the triangle carefully and identify the reference angle.
Label the hypotenuse first. Then label the opposite and adjacent sides relative to the chosen angle. This prevents one of the most common beginner mistakes.
Next ask: which two sides do I know or need? That immediately points to sine, cosine, or tangent. Write the equation symbolically before inserting numbers.
Finally, solve the equation, check whether the result is reasonable, include the correct unit for a length, and round only at the end if the problem asks for rounding.
The Pythagorean theorem and trigonometric ratios are two different tools for right triangles, but they work together naturally.
For a right triangle with legs \(a\) and \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\), the Pythagorean theorem says:
If you know two sides, the Pythagorean theorem can give the third. If you know an acute angle and a suitable side, a trigonometric ratio can give another side.
Knowing which tool fits the information you have is an important part of solving triangle problems efficiently.
The angles in every triangle add to \(180^\circ\). A right triangle already contains \(90^\circ\), so its two acute angles must add to another \(90^\circ\).
Therefore, if one acute angle is \(	heta\), the other is \(90^\circ-	heta\). These are called complementary angles.
When you switch from one acute angle to the other, the opposite and adjacent sides swap roles. This explains why sine and cosine are connected by complementary angles:
\[\sin(	heta)=\cos(90^\circ-	heta)\]
\[\cos(	heta)=\sin(90^\circ-	heta)\]

sections.title: Why Tangent Equals Sine Divided by Cosine

content.text: The relationship between tangent, sine, and cosine follows directly from their definitions.
Start with the two ratios:
\[\sin(	heta)= rac{O}{H},\qquad \cos(	heta)= rac{A}{H}\]
Divide sine by cosine:
\[ rac{\sin(	heta)}{\cos(	heta)}= rac{O/H}{A/H}= rac{O}{A}\]
But \( rac{O}{A}=	an(	heta)\). Therefore:
\[	an(	heta)= rac{\sin(	heta)}{\cos(	heta)}\]

sections.title: Why Triangle Size Does Not Matter

content.text: Imagine multiplying every side of a triangle by the same scale factor \(k\). The opposite side becomes \(kO\), and the hypotenuse becomes \(kH\).
The sine ratio becomes \( rac{kO}{kH}\). The common factor \(k\) cancels, leaving \( rac{O}{H}\).
The same argument works for cosine and tangent. This is the mathematical reason a trigonometric ratio belongs to an angle rather than to one particular triangle.
When the angle is given in degrees, your calculator must be in degree mode. If it is in radian mode, the numerical values will be different.
For example, when evaluating \(\sin(30^\circ)\), the calculator should interpret \(30\) as \(30^\circ\), not as \(30\) radians.
A useful habit is to check the calculator display for DEG before starting a problem involving degree measures.
Calculators are useful for numerical values, but the mathematical reasoning should come first: identify the sides, select the ratio, write the equation, and only then calculate.

sections.title: Checking Whether Your Answer Makes Sense

content.text: A calculator can give you a number, but it cannot tell you whether your setup was correct. Always perform a quick reasonableness check.
For an acute angle, \(0<\sin(	heta)<1\) and \(0<\cos(	heta)<1\). Tangent is positive and may be greater than \(1\).
The hypotenuse must be longer than either leg. If your calculation says a hypotenuse is shorter than a leg, something is wrong.
If the angle is relatively small, the opposite side should generally be relatively small compared with the hypotenuse. If the angle is large, the opposite side should be relatively large.
Most beginner right-triangle problems fall into three patterns. First, you may be asked to calculate a trigonometric ratio when the relevant side lengths are known.
Second, you may know an angle and one side and be asked to find another side. In this case, choose the ratio containing the known and unknown sides and rearrange the equation.
Third, you may be asked to solve several missing side lengths in a right triangle. You can combine trigonometric ratios with the Pythagorean theorem as needed.
The key skill across all three is translating the geometry of the triangle into the correct ratio.

sections.title: The Bigger Idea: Ratios Become Functions

content.text: At this stage, sine, cosine, and tangent can be understood as ratios in right triangles. There is a deeper viewpoint coming next: each ratio can be treated as a function whose input is an angle.
That means an angle can be the input and a numerical ratio can be the output. For example, \(\sin(30^\circ)= rac{1}{2}\).
Later, this function viewpoint will let us study trigonometry beyond a single right triangle, including graphs, periodic behaviour, and angles outside the acute-angle setting.

formulas.name: Sine Ratio
formulas.explanation: Sine compares the opposite side with the hypotenuse.

formulas.name: Cosine Ratio
formulas.explanation: Cosine compares the adjacent side with the hypotenuse.

formulas.name: Tangent Ratio
formulas.explanation: Tangent compares the opposite side with the adjacent side.

formulas.name: Tangent Relationship
formulas.explanation: Dividing the sine ratio by the cosine ratio cancels the hypotenuse.

formulas.name: Complementary-Angle Relationship
formulas.explanation: The opposite side for one acute angle becomes the adjacent side for its complementary angle.

formulas.name: Complementary-Angle Relationship
formulas.explanation: The adjacent side for one acute angle becomes the opposite side for its complementary angle.

formulas.name: Pythagorean Theorem
formulas.explanation: For a right triangle, the squares of the two legs add to the square of the hypotenuse.

examples.question: A right triangle has an opposite side of 6 cm and a hypotenuse of 10 cm. Find \(\sin(\theta)\).
examples.solution: Use sine because the opposite side and hypotenuse are known. \[\sin(\theta)=\frac{6}{10}=\frac{3}{5}=0.6\]

examples.question: A right triangle has an adjacent side of 8 cm and a hypotenuse of 10 cm. Find \(\cos(\theta)\).
examples.solution: Use cosine because the adjacent side and hypotenuse are known. \[\cos(\theta)=\frac{8}{10}=\frac{4}{5}=0.8\]

examples.question: A right triangle has an opposite side of 9 cm and an adjacent side of 12 cm. Find \(\tan(\theta)\).
examples.solution: Use tangent because the opposite and adjacent sides are known. \[\tan(\theta)=\frac{9}{12}=\frac{3}{4}=0.75\]

examples.question: A right triangle has an angle of \(30^\circ\) and a hypotenuse of 12 cm. Find the opposite side.
examples.solution: The opposite side and hypotenuse belong in the sine ratio. \[\sin(30^\circ)=\frac{x}{12}\] Since \(\sin(30^\circ)=\frac{1}{2}\), we get \(\frac{1}{2}=\frac{x}{12}\). Therefore \(x=6\,\text{cm}\).

examples.question: A right triangle has an angle of \(60^\circ\) and an adjacent side of 5 cm. Find the hypotenuse.
examples.solution: The adjacent side and hypotenuse belong in the cosine ratio. \[\cos(60^\circ)=\frac{5}{h}\] Since \(\cos(60^\circ)=\frac{1}{2}\), \(\frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{h}\). Cross-multiplying gives \(h=10\,\text{cm}\).

examples.question: A right triangle has an angle of \(45^\circ\) and an adjacent side of 7 cm. Find the opposite side.
examples.solution: Use tangent because opposite and adjacent are involved. \[\tan(45^\circ)=\frac{x}{7}\] Since \(\tan(45^\circ)=1\), we have \(1=\frac{x}{7}\), so \(x=7\,\text{cm}\).

examples.question: A right triangle has an angle of \(30^\circ\) and an adjacent side of 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse.
A right triangle has an angle of \(45^\circ\) and a hypotenuse of 10 cm. Find the adjacent side.
A right triangle has legs of 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the hypotenuse and the three basic ratios for the angle opposite the 6 cm side.
examples.solution: Use the Pythagorean theorem first: \[h^2=6^2+8^2=36+64=100\] so \(h=10\,\text{cm}\). For the angle opposite the 6 cm side, opposite = 6, adjacent = 8, hypotenuse = 10. Therefore \[\sin(\theta)=\frac{3}{5},\qquad \cos(\theta)=\frac{4}{5},\qquad \tan(\theta)=\frac{3}{4}.\]

examples.question: Two similar right triangles have the same acute angle. In the first triangle, the opposite side is 4 cm and the hypotenuse is 10 cm. In the second, the hypotenuse is 15 cm. Find the corresponding opposite side.
examples.solution: Because the triangles are similar, the sine ratio is unchanged. \[\frac{4}{10}=\frac{x}{15}\] Multiply both sides by 15: \(x=15\cdot\frac{4}{10}=6\,\text{cm}.\)

key_ideas: Trigonometry connects angles with side-length relationships in triangles.
A right triangle contains one \(90^\circ\) angle; its opposite side is the hypotenuse and is always the longest side.
Opposite and adjacent are defined relative to the chosen acute angle.
Similar right triangles with the same acute angle have the same side ratios.
SOH-CAH-TOA is a memory aid, not a replacement for understanding the definitions.
A trigonometric equation can be rearranged using ordinary algebra to find an unknown side.
For a right triangle, the two acute angles are complementary.
A calculator should be in degree mode when the problem gives angles in degrees.
Always check whether a numerical answer is geometrically reasonable.
misconceptions: Opposite and adjacent are not permanent labels; they depend on the angle being studied.
The hypotenuse is identified by the \(90^\circ\) angle, not simply by choosing the longest-looking side.
Tangent does not use the hypotenuse.
Sine and cosine are ratios, not lengths. They do not have centimetres or metres as units.
The same acute angle can occur in triangles of many different sizes, but the corresponding trigonometric ratios stay the same.
SOH-CAH-TOA does not tell you which angle to use; you must identify the reference angle first.
A calculator result is not automatically correct; an incorrect ratio setup can still produce a precise number.
Do not round intermediate values unnecessarily because early rounding can affect the final answer.
For acute angles, sine and cosine are between 0 and 1, but tangent can be greater than 1.
The hypotenuse cannot be shorter than either leg.
